overview: The modern Republic of Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991. War and territorial disputes marked its first years, with peaceful reintegration of the remaining eastern region completed in January 1998. It later joined the European Union and adopted the euro. This entry is distinct from the medieval Croatian kingdom.

periods.title: Independence, war and reintegration
periods.summary: Croatia became independent amid war; UN administration helped complete peaceful reintegration of the eastern region in 1998.

periods.title: After reintegration
periods.summary: The end of the UN transitional administration marked a major step in restoring state administration across Croatia.

periods.title: An EU member state
periods.summary: Croatia joined the European Union in 2013 and the euro area in 2023.

items.text: Peaceful reintegration in eastern Croatia involved more than transferring offices. UN reporting discussed pensions, welfare payments, policing, returning residents and protection of rights. Restoring daily routines and trust was part of the work of bringing a war-affected region back under Croatian administration.

The Pelješac Bridge opened in July 2022. Its approximately 2.4-kilometer crossing carries four lanes of road traffic, while its height allows ships to pass below. Roads and sea routes meet at the same structure, so engineers had to make room for both.

The Zagreb earthquake of March 2020 damaged hundreds of education buildings. Schools were already closed because of the pandemic, so pupils were not in classrooms when it struck. The damage assessment estimated that thousands would need different teaching locations while buildings were repaired.

Croatia joined the European Union in 2013 and began using euro coins and banknotes in January 2023. Currency change affected ordinary shopping and household budgets as well as banks. A familiar price tag now had a different unit printed beside the number.

Primary schooling is compulsory and free, lasting at least eight years. Children can also attend separate music or dance programs alongside general school. A pupil’s week may therefore include both ordinary classroom subjects and time learning an instrument or practicing dance.

A bronze statue of an ancient athlete was raised from the seabed near Lošinj in 1999. Croatian and Italian specialists spent six years conserving it. The statue belongs to antiquity, but recovering, studying and displaying it was a modern achievement in archaeological conservation.

Researchers found a rodent’s nest inside the hollow bronze, probably made by a field mouse, along with laurel leaves and fruit remains. These small traces became part of the statue’s story. For a while, an artwork that would eventually receive its own museum had also served as somebody’s very unusual mouse house.

Wooden toy makers in Hrvatsko Zagorje use local woods such as willow, lime, beech and maple. UNESCO’s account describes family production, with men traditionally carving and women painting. Each toy is handmade, so matching horses or whistles may have small differences.

The toy repertoire has expanded to include cars, airplanes and other modern forms, alongside horses and miniature furniture. Some toys are tuned musical instruments used in children’s learning. A living craft can keep familiar techniques while changing what children get to play with.

Decorated gingerbread hearts from northern Croatia often carry a little mirror and a written message. They can be gifts expressing affection or respect. The decoration matters as much as the dough: this is a craft of making a keepsake for another person.

Gingerbread makers have passed their skills through family workshops, historically connected with candle making and honey drinks. Metal molds gradually replaced wooden ones, but individual decoration remained important. A shared outline could still become a distinctive gift in a maker’s hands.

Croatian, article 1 of the constitution: “Republika Hrvatska jedinstvena je i nedjeljiva demokratska i socijalna država.” Translation: “The Republic of Croatia is a unified and indivisible democratic and social state.” This is the Constitutional Court’s 2014 consolidated witness of the constitution first enacted in 1990.

ending.text: The Republic of Croatia continues. The map’s 1994 starting point falls after independence and during the war, not at the state’s founding. Peaceful reintegration of the eastern region concluded on 15 January 1998, while rebuilding lives and institutions extended beyond that administrative milestone.
